newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Italian troops arrive in anarchic Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italian troops arrive in anarchic Albania.

text.p: Italian soldiers arrived in Albania on Friday to spearhead a multinational force that aims to secure key harbours and Tirana's airport in the Balkan country racked by weeks of armed anarchy.

A first wave of 20 Italian troops on a transport ship marched onto a pier in the western port of Durres just after dawn. Four Lockheed C130 Hercules aircraft carrying more than 50 paratroopers landed within hours at Tirana's airport.

The Italian troops were preparing the ground for a 6,000-strong force from six nations that is due to start arriving in Albania on Monday. Soldiers from France, Spain, Romania, Turkey and Greece are coming to Albania to help safeguard deliveries of emergency food and medical supplies.

"Our mission does not rule out risks, but we hope the Albanian people will understand that we are here to help them," said Colonel Enrico Nardi, commander of the Italian landing unit in Durres, 40 (25 miles) west of Tirana.

"We plan to check the road between Durres and Tirana and perhaps the airport," he added. Armed gangs fought pitched gun battles with police and each other last month in Durres, the country's second largest city.
More than 200 people have been killed since rebels took control of the south last month in an eruption of anger following the collapse of a number of pyramid savings schemes.
Army arsenals were looted after soldiers and police abandoned their posts while automatic rifles and weapons were seized by citizens who brandished them on streets.

The Italian troops, part of the first multinational mission led by Italy since World War Two, arrived in Durres smiling. They talked with journalists for about an hour. Standing under clear blue skies on the pier next to the brilliant turquoise Adriatic, they also handed pieces of candy to local children.

Only a handful of Albanians, who have been waiting for more than one month in vain for international help, were on hand to witness the Italians' arrival. The mission has attracted little attention in the local media.

"All this for only 20 soldiers?" asked a 50-year-old port worker named Besim as he watched some 40 foreign journalists and camera crews scramble to interview the soldiers on the pier. "There are more journalists than soldiers."

The Italian naval vessel, the Pantellaria, that carried the advance unit was escorted by a small Italian minesweeper, the Rimini. They steamed into Durres shortly after 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) and the minesweeper returned to Italy.

It took the Pantellaria about 30 minutes to get its gangplank lined up on the shore. Five military vehicles armed with roof-mounted machine guns drove off first, followed by the rest of the 20 soldiers.
Although Albania has been racked by weeks of near anarchy and armed banditry, Durres' port has been quiet for several weeks and regular passenger ferry traffic to Italy was resumed two weeks ago.
"I don't thing they are going to attack us, because they need us," said an Italian lieutenant named Sandro, who declined to provide his surname. "We want to help our Albanian friends."

Asked by one Italian reporter if he knew that Italy's fascist leader Benito Mussolini sent troops to occupy Albania through the Durres port 58 years ago this month, another officer, a captain named Giorgio, shrugged his shoulders.
"I don't know what happened then, but I am sure we are here to help people in need," he said.

The soldiers at Tirana airport included a team of special forces with orders to secure the perimeter and a group of specialists whose job is to ensure the airport can operate round the clock and not just during daylight hours as at present.

The dispatch of the troops had been warmly welcomed by Albanian leaders, whose original call for a large-scale international intervention force to restore order was rejected by the West. But Prime Minister Bashkim Fino's office said they had no immediate comment on the troops' arrival.
Separately, Albania's Education Minister said he expected the country's schools and universities, closed since a wave of armed violence swept the country, could reopen in about 10 days.

Also, two independent daily newspapers in Tirana put out their first editions in a month on Friday, raising to four the number of dailies that have returned after parliament relaxed restrictions on the local media this week.
